newsReadings.title: A Record October: What a Super El Niño Means for a Warming World
newsReadings.source: Scientific American, 'This October is on track to be the hottest ever recorded,' 30 October 2026
newsReadings.passage:
This October is almost certainly going to be the hottest October ever recorded. Global temperatures this month are set to be around 1.76 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, surpassing the previous record set in 2023, according to projections by climate scientists Andrew Dessler and Zeke Hausfather based on data from the Europe-based Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). If the projection holds, it will cap a year already crowded with superlatives: the United States has experienced its hottest September, its hottest first eight months and its hottest 12-month period ever recorded, while global ocean temperatures have also reached unprecedented highs.

The immediate driver, the researchers argue, is not a mystery. A powerful El Niño is taking hold. El Niño is a cyclic climate pattern that occurs when part of the Pacific Ocean becomes unusually warm, redistributing heat and altering weather patterns across the world. On its own, it can raise global average temperatures for a year or more. Combined with the long-term warming caused by the burning of fossil fuels, however, its effect is amplified: the background warming provides a higher baseline, and El Niño adds a further pulse of heat on top. Hausfather describes the current event as a 'Super El Niño' kicking into gear, and warns that this October may be merely the first in a series of record-setting months, culminating in a record-setting 2027.

The comparison with 2023 is instructive. That year was also an El Niño year, and its October reached about 1.7 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels — a figure that seemed extraordinary at the time. That the new record exceeds it by a measurable margin, rather than merely matching it, suggests that the underlying trend has not paused. Each successive El Niño now unfolds against a warmer background than the last, so records that once stood for decades are being broken within a few years. For scientists, this compression of timescales is itself a signal: it indicates that natural variability is operating on top of, not instead of, sustained human-caused warming.

Why does a single month matter? A monthly record, on its own, does not prove a trend, and climatologists are careful to distinguish weather from climate. Yet October's figure is significant for three reasons. First, it is consistent with a broader pattern: the past eleven years have been the warmest on record, and the oceans — which absorb the vast majority of excess heat — have never been warmer. Second, the record is occurring before the El Niño has fully peaked, which implies that further warming may still be in store. Third, the heat is not abstract. Higher baseline temperatures intensify heatwaves, prolong droughts, increase the moisture the atmosphere can hold and therefore the intensity of rainfall, and raise sea levels through thermal expansion and ice melt. The costs are felt in harvests, insurance bills, hospital admissions and the habitability of entire regions.

None of this means that the future is predetermined. The same science that attributes the warming also identifies its principal cause, and therefore its principal remedy: reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The difference between a world that stabilises near current temperatures and one that continues upward depends on decisions taken in the next few years — about energy systems, land use and the pace at which fossil fuels are replaced. International negotiations, including the forthcoming COP31 climate summit, are framed precisely around that choice: whether pledges made on paper translate into measurable reductions in the atmosphere.

For now, October's likely record serves as both a warning and a measure. It warns that the climate system responds quickly when a natural warming pulse is superimposed on human-caused warming. It measures, with unusual clarity, how far the baseline has already moved. The question that follows is not whether another record will come — on current trends, it almost certainly will — but whether societies will treat each broken record as a surprise, or as the predictable consequence of a system they still have the power to change.

questions.q: What do Dessler and Hausfather project for October 2026?
options: That it will be the coldest October on record
That global temperatures will be around 1.76°C above preindustrial levels, surpassing the 2023 record
That temperatures will fall below preindustrial levels
That no record will be set

questions.q: What is El Niño, according to the passage?
options: A permanent change in ocean currents
A cyclic pattern in which part of the Pacific becomes unusually warm, altering weather worldwide

questions.q: The passage states that October 2023 reached about 1.7°C above preindustrial levels.
Why is the new record especially significant, according to the passage?
options: Because each El Niño now unfolds against a warmer background, so records are broken within a few years
Because El Niño has stopped occurring
Because fossil fuel burning has ended

questions.q: According to the passage, higher baseline temperatures have no effect on rainfall intensity.
Why does the passage say October matters despite being a single month?
options: It fits a broader pattern of record warmth, occurs before El Niño has peaked, and reflects tangible impacts such as heatwaves and sea-level rise
It is the only warm month on record

questions.q: What does the passage identify as the principal remedy for warming?
options: Waiting for El Niño to end

questions.q: The passage claims that a record-setting 2027 is guaranteed.

newsReadings.title: Reading the Ocean's Carbon Ledger: Why 'Ocean Carbon Intelligence' Matters
newsReadings.source: UNEP press release, 'UN report urges investment in Ocean Carbon Intelligence to safeguard the ocean's climate role,' 28 October 2026
newsReadings.passage:
The ocean is one of humanity's most important climate allies, and one of its least understood. It absorbs around 30 per cent of human-induced carbon dioxide emissions and approximately 90 per cent of the excess heat generated by climate change. Without that service, atmospheric warming would already be far more severe, and the pace of climate change would be visibly faster. Yet the very processes that make the ocean such a powerful buffer are themselves being altered by warming, acidification and other pressures — a paradox at the heart of a new United Nations report released in Copenhagen on 28 October 2026.

The report, the UN's 2026 Climate Technology Progress Report, introduces a concept it calls Ocean Carbon Intelligence: a framework that connects ocean science, monitoring technologies, data infrastructure and analytical tools to improve understanding of ocean carbon dynamics and support evidence-based climate action. Produced by the UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre in collaboration with the Climate Technology Centre and Network and the Technology Executive Committee of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the report argues that governments, researchers and investors cannot manage what they cannot measure. As interest grows in ocean-based climate solutions, from restoring coastal ecosystems to removing carbon dioxide directly from seawater, the gaps in observation and modelling become not a technical footnote but a strategic risk.

Those gaps are substantial. The ocean is vast, deep and difficult to observe continuously; much of its carbon cycle operates far below the surface, in currents and ecosystems that satellites alone cannot capture. Existing monitoring networks leave large regions sparsely sampled, and the data that do exist are often fragmented across institutions, formats and national boundaries. Modelling must then fill the blanks, but models are only as reliable as the observations that calibrate them. When a policymaker asks how much carbon a restored mangrove forest will store over twenty years, or whether a proposed marine carbon removal technique will work at scale without unintended side effects, an approximate answer is not enough. Investment decisions worth billions of dollars, and climate targets that depend on them, rest on numbers whose uncertainty is still too large.

The report therefore calls for sustained investment in three linked areas: ocean observation, data infrastructure and modelling. Observation means more sensors, more sustained measurements and better coverage of under-sampled regions, including the deep ocean and the Southern Ocean. Data infrastructure means systems that make those measurements findable, comparable and usable across countries and disciplines, rather than locked in incompatible archives. Modelling means tools that can translate observations into projections decision-makers can trust — for example, how the ocean's capacity to absorb carbon may change as it warms, and at what point that capacity begins to weaken. The authors warn explicitly that climate change is already affecting the ocean's ability to absorb and store carbon; the buffer cannot be assumed to behave in the future as it has in the past.

Ocean Carbon Intelligence is also presented as a safeguard for the solutions themselves. Blue carbon ecosystem restoration — the protection and recovery of mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes — is widely regarded as promising, because these ecosystems store carbon densely and provide fisheries, coastal protection and biodiversity benefits at the same time. Emerging marine carbon dioxide removal approaches, by contrast, are newer and less proven, and their risks are less well characterised. Both categories, the report argues, require the same discipline: baseline measurements before intervention, monitoring during deployment, and independent verification afterwards. Without that discipline, a project may claim climate benefits it has not delivered, or cause ecological harm that goes undetected until it is too late to reverse.

The stakes extend beyond climate accounting. Coastal communities depend on the ocean for food, livelihoods and protection from storms; changes in its chemistry and temperature ripple through fisheries, coral reefs and the weather systems that shape rainfall on land. A weakened ocean carbon sink would not merely make climate targets harder to reach — it would accelerate warming itself, creating a feedback loop in which a diminished buffer leads to faster warming, which further diminishes the buffer. Breaking that loop requires, first, seeing it clearly.

That is the report's central message: intelligence before intervention. The ocean has quietly absorbed a large share of humanity's emissions for decades, subsidising the delay in cutting them. As governments prepare for COP31 and weigh ocean-based solutions alongside emissions cuts, the report urges them to invest in the science that makes those choices honest. To protect the ocean's climate role, it argues, the world must first learn to read its carbon ledger with precision — and then act on what the ledger shows.

questions.q: According to the report, how much human-induced CO₂ and excess heat does the ocean absorb?
options: About 10% of CO₂ and 50% of excess heat
Around 30% of CO₂ and approximately 90% of excess heat
Around 90% of CO₂ and 30% of excess heat
A framework linking ocean science, monitoring technologies, data infrastructure and analytical tools to understand ocean carbon dynamics
A method for removing all carbon from seawater

questions.q: The report was produced solely by UNEP without any collaborators.
Why are gaps in ocean observation described as a strategic risk?
options: Because investment decisions and climate targets rest on uncertain numbers about how much carbon solutions will store
Because the ocean contains no carbon
Because all ocean data is already complete

questions.q: Which three areas does the report call for sustained investment in?
options: Ocean observation, data infrastructure and modelling

questions.q: The report warns that climate change is already affecting the ocean's ability to absorb and store carbon.
What discipline does the report require for both blue carbon restoration and marine carbon removal?
options: Baseline measurements before intervention, monitoring during deployment, and independent verification afterwards
Only claiming benefits after the project ends

questions.q: What is the report's central message?
options: Intervene in the ocean before measuring anything
Intelligence before intervention: learn to read the ocean's carbon ledger precisely, then act on it
Emissions cuts are unnecessary if ocean solutions expand
